stem:
A 56-year-old woman has a morphine PCA after hysterectomy. She is comfortable, easily roused and breathing normally at 14/min. Her partner tells the ward nurse that he pressed the button while she slept last night, because the night before she woke at 3 am in severe pain. He asks what he should do tonight instead.

Which plan is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: He presses only when she wakes and asks for it
options.explanation: Even a requested press by another person bypasses the sedation safeguard, because she may ask while drowsy or before the previous dose has peaked. Only the patient should activate the PCA.

options.label: B
options.text: Add a background infusion to cover sleep
options.explanation: Background infusions in opioid-naive adults add little analgesia and increase the risk of respiratory depression, particularly during sleep.

options.label: C
options.text: Only she presses; the pain team reviews it
options.explanation: PCA is safe because a patient who becomes sedated stops pressing. Any dose given by someone else removes that safeguard. Waking in pain is a real problem, but the answer is a review of the regimen (for example regular non-opioid adjuncts), not proxy dosing.

options.label: D
options.text: Shorten the lockout so she can catch up
options.explanation: A shorter lockout allows doses to stack before each has peaked, increasing the risk of sedation; it does not address night-time pain safely.

options.label: E
options.text: He presses if she looks restless asleep
options.explanation: Restlessness during sleep is not a reliable sign of pain and can reflect hypoxia or airway obstruction. Pressing for a sleeping patient is exactly the proxy dosing that causes overdose.

context: Only the patient should press a PCA button, so that sedation stops further doses. Pain that breaks through during sleep calls for a review of the regimen, not proxy dosing or a background infusion.
